blocks.text: VIII. The eighth is Psal. L, 11., where the Hebrew has I know every bird of the mountains, וזיז שדי עמדי, and the ziz of the field is with me. And the Chaldee has: Before me are open all the kinds of birds that fly in the air of the heavens, ותרנגול ברא דקרצולי שרין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא, and the wild cock, whose legs stand on the ground, and whose head reaches the heavens.

IX. And the ninth is Psal. LXXX, 14., where for the Hebrew וזיז שדה ירענה, And the ziz of the field has grazed it bare, the Chaldee again has ותרנגולא ברא יתפרנס מנה, And the wild cock shall feed on it. As if the Hebrew זיז ziz meant a cock, and indeed that cock about which so much is said. But in the chapter On the Boar we have shown that זיז ziz in Hebrew is a wild beast, and is so called from its motion, like the Greek κνώδαλα [knōdala] and κινώπετα [kinōpeta]. So neither of these passages has anything to do with the cock.

[II, 684] X. The tenth passage is Prov. XXX, 31., where Solomon calls some animal of magnificent gait, by periphrasis (περιφραστικῶς [periphrastikōs]), זרזיר מתנים, girded in the loins. For verses 29, 30, 31 read thus: There are three things of fine gait, indeed four that step handsomely: the lion, strongest of animals, who turns back before no one; the one girded in the loins; and the he-goat; and the king, against whom no one rises up. And there the words זרזיר מתנים, that is, girded in the loins, are rendered by the Greeks with remarkable freedom as ἀλεκτὼρ ἐμπεριπατῶν θηλείαις εὐψύχως [alektōr emperipatōn thēleiais eupsychōs], a cock walking briskly among the females. And by the Arabic translator: الديك اذا تمشا بين الاناث من الدجاج بطيبة النفس [al-dīk idhā tamashshā bayna al-ināth min al-dajāj bi-ṭībat al-nafs], The cock, when he walks among the female hens with briskness of spirit. And also by the Syriac: ܐܒܟܐ ܕܡܬܪܘܪܒ ܒܝܢܬ ܬܪܢܓܠܬܐ, A cock walking proudly among the hens. If you compare these with the Chaldee version, from which they were drawn, you will find that three errors have crept into it. For the Chaldee version reads אכבא דמודרז בינת תרנגולי, for which one should write אבכא דמזדרכל בינת תרנגולן. By the Chaldeans and Syrians the cock is called ܬܪܢܓܘܠ tarnegol. Nowhere otherwise, as far as I remember, except in this one passage, where for cock the Syriac has ܐܒܟܐ abacha, and the Chaldee אכבא achaba. Accordingly the Baal Aruch passed over the word אכבא achaba without concern. And Elias admits that he does not understand it. Others explain it as cock. I prefer to write it with the Syriac ܐܒܟܐ abacha, rather than with the Chaldee אכבא achaba. For if it is written אכבא achaba, it will be of unknown origin. But ܐܒܟܐ abacha comes from the verb אבך abach, whose Hithphael התאבך hithabach means to be lifted up and to be exalted, Es. IX, 18. Hence the cock seems to have been called ܐܒܟܐ abacha, a most fitting name, and one that exactly expresses the nature of this bird. For, if you except the peacock, no bird is prouder than the cock. Hence Pliny, book 10, chapter 21, after treating the pride of the peacock, says: Next to them, these night-watchmen of ours also have a sense of glory, whom nature has produced to rouse mortals to their work and to break their sleep. And a little later: But if the palm (in the fight) falls to them, they at once crow in victory and proclaim themselves the masters. The vanquished hides in silence and bears servitude with difficulty. And yet the common sort too struts with equal pride, neck held high, lofty with its crest, and alone of the birds it often looks up at the sky, raising aloft also its sickle-shaped tail. These are so many signs of pride. And Aelian, Hist. book 4, ch. 29: Κρατήσας δὲ γαῦρός ἐστι, καὶ ὑψαυχενεῖν, καὶ [col. 117] κυδρουμένῳ ἔοικεν [Kratēsas de gauros esti, kai hypsauchenein, kai kydroumenō eoiken] (read ὑψαυχενῶν, καὶ κυδρουμένῳ ἐοικὼς [hypsauchenōn, kai kydroumenō eoikōs]), When he has won he is proud, with neck erect, and like one who glories. And Philes, chapter 12:

Ἀλεκτρυὼν μέν τοι γε νικῶν τὴν μάχην Σφριγᾷ τε καθαρῶς, καὶ σοβεῖ, καὶ τέρπεται· [Alektryōn men toi ge nikōn tēn machēn / Sphriga te katharōs, kai sobei, kai terpetai] [II, 685] The cock, when he has the upper hand in the fight, fairly swells, and struts with pomp and exults. And Basil, Hexaëmeron, Homily 8: Γαῦρον ὁ ἀλεκτρυὼν, Φιλόκαλον ὁ ταὼς, λάγναι αἱ περιστεραί· [Gauron ho alektryōn, Philokalon ho taōs, lagnai hai peristerai] The cock is a proud thing, the peacock fond of elegance, doves lustful. Lucilius, book 8 of the Satires:
When the victorious barnyard cock has proudly raised himself onto his toes and lifts up the tips of his claws.
